newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ECNZ sees price volatility in wholesale market.
newsitem.headline: ECNZ sees price volatility in wholesale market.

text.p: Electricity prices in New Zealand will undoubtedly be volatile in the new wholesale market which begins next week, Electricity Corporation of New Zealand said on Thursday.
The country's largest generator of electricity also declared the tendering of its long-term electricity contracts an overwhelming success.

"I think the fact that there is a new regime that comes into effect from the first of October, and a likelihood that there will be more volatility in the price of electricity, has probably encouraged buyers to participate strongly," ECNZ general manager of marketing Peter Larsen said in an interview.
About 94 percent of the volume on offer was allocated to bidders, securing around NZ$1.4 billion in revenue over a five year period for the state-owned generator.
Eighty percent of ECNZ's total generation is now allocated in contracts for the next 12 months, leaving only 20 percent exposed to the new spot market, down from 38 percent previously.

Under a memorandum of understanding with the government, ECNZ, which dominates the generation industry with a 67 percent market share, is obligated to offer set percentages of its firm capacity by tender though long-term contracts.

"In effect, we have to have contracts that go out at least five years in the market at any one point in time, so we will continue to offer contracts on an on-going basis until such time as our market share reduces to 45 percent," Larsen said.
But the contracts are also a boon for ECNZ.

"We have the opportunity to write contracts with our customers more than 12 months in advance. We have never had long-term contracts out of the market before. I think the final outcome for ECNZ is greater revenue certainty," Larsen said.
The new market will bring many changes, among them the scrapping of a price cap on electricity.
Previously, the effective cost of producing the most expensive unit of electricity -- through diesel-fired generation -- placed a cap on price of about 16 cents per unit.
"It is true that the cap has been removed, which was artificially established under the previous regime," said Larsen.

"There will be strong competition in terms of offering capacity into the (market) pool, and people's offering behaviour will depend on their ability to generate and the contract cover that they have," he said.
"The resulting spot price will fluctuate without a doubt. Whether it fluctuates beyond the previously set artificial cap will depend on the forces of supply and demand at that time."
ECNZ's contract tender clearing prices for the next 12 months were about 1.0 to 1.5 percent higher than current prices and increased about six percent over a five-year period.
Larsen said he was absolutely confident that true competition would emerge between ECNZ and the other state-owned generator, Contact Energy, which would act to keep prices down.

"The wholesale market will see competition between generators in terms of offering their capacity into the pool and the benefit for consumers should be a price for electricity that buyers and sellers agree upon," Larsen said.
